title: Introduction to Quarto
text: Introduction to Quarto

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Before the workshop
Please finish these steps before the workshop so we can spend our time together on Quarto itself. They take about 15 minutes.
This setup builds on the Git workshop. It assumes you already have:

Git installed (on Windows, this gave you Git Bash)
A GitHub account
An SSH key connecting your computer to GitHub

Type every command below in a terminal: Terminal on macOS or Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or the terminal inside RStudio.

Step 1: Install Quarto
Download the installer for your operating system from https://quarto.org/docs/download/ and run it.
RStudio comes with its own copy of Quarto, but please install Quarto separately anyway. The separate install works in any terminal, and it lets you control which version you have. You won’t break anything: RStudio will use your installed copy automatically.
When the installer finishes, close any open terminals and restart RStudio so they can find Quarto.


Step 2: Check your Quarto version
Open a new terminal and run:
quarto --version
You need version 1.9 or higher. Earlier versions can’t publish to Posit Connect Cloud from the terminal, which we will do in the workshop.
If you don’t see a version number of 1.9 or higher:

command not found: Quarto isn’t installed, or the terminal can’t find it yet. Re-run the installer, then open a new terminal and try again.
A version lower than 1.9: your terminal is finding an older copy of Quarto, often one installed for an earlier course. Run which quarto to see where that copy lives. Then download the current installer from the link above, run it, and check the version again in a new terminal.

For a fuller diagnosis, quarto check reports which version of Quarto you are running and whether it can find R and Python.


Step 3: Create a Posit Connect Cloud account
Posit Connect Cloud is a free service for sharing documents online. We will publish a report and a slide deck to it during the workshop.

Go to https://connect.posit.cloud/
Click Sign Up
Choose to sign up with GitHub, using the GitHub account you already have

The free plan is all you need. If you already have an account, you can skip this step.


Step 4: Create your workshop repo on GitHub
During the workshop you will build a small project about ice cover on Lake Mendota. Make a home for it on GitHub now.
In your browser, signed in to GitHub:

Click + (top right) → New repository
Name it mendota_ice
Choose Public or Private; either works
From the Add .gitignore dropdown, choose the R template
Click Create repository

Don’t skip the .gitignore. It tells Git to ignore the clutter that R and RStudio create (like .Rhistory and .Rproj.user/). It also gives the repo its first commit, so when you clone it, git push and git pull work right away.


Step 5: Clone the repo to your computer
On your new repo’s page, click the green Code button, select the SSH tab, and copy the address.
In your terminal, move to the folder where you keep your GitHub repos. We used ~/github in the Git workshop; use your own folder if it’s different. Then clone the repo, pasting your own address:
cd ~/github
git clone git@github.com:your_username/mendota_ice.git
Move into the new folder and look around:
cd mendota_ice
ls -a
.  ..  .git  .gitignore
You should see the .gitignore you created on GitHub, plus the hidden .git folder that holds the repo’s history.


Step 6: Download the data and references
Our report will use 170 years of ice records for Lake Mendota, and our paper will cite them. Put a copy of the data in a data folder inside your repo, and the reference file (refs.bib) at the top of your repo.
Stay in your mendota_ice folder. Copy the three commands below (use the copy button at the top right of the box), paste them into your terminal, and press Enter:
mkdir data
curl -fsSL -o data/mendota_ice.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjcurtin/book_quarto/main/data/mendota_ice.csv
curl -fsSL -o refs.bib https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjcurtin/book_quarto/main/refs.bib
mkdir makes the data folder. Each curl command downloads one file. If all goes well, none of the commands prints anything.
Check that the files arrived:
head -3 data/mendota_ice.csv
head -1 refs.bib
winter,year,ice_days
1855-56,1856,118
1856-57,1857,151
@dataset{magnuson2026,
If you see an error instead, make sure you are in your mendota_ice folder (pwd shows where you are), then paste the commands again. If mkdir says the folder already exists, that’s fine; just run the two curl lines.
That’s it. You’re ready for the workshop. We will start from this folder.

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.1 Why are we here?
By the end of this hour you will be able to:
You’ll build along with me the whole hour, with a few Your turn moments to try a step on your own.
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
Explain what Quarto is and how it works with R and RStudio
Write a report that mixes text and R code
Render it to a self-contained file and publish it online
Turn the same kind of document into a slide deck
Write a manuscript with citations and cross-references
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.2 What is Quarto?
Quarto is a free, open-source publishing system.



You write one plain-text file (a .qmd) that mixes:

Text, written in markdown
Code, in R or Python
A few options at the top, written in YAML




Quarto turns that file into a finished document:

Reports (HTML, Word, PDF)
Slide decks
Manuscripts and journal articles
Posters, websites, dashboards (these are not covered today)
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.3 R, RStudio, and Quarto
Three tools, three different jobs:











Tool
What it is
Its job




R (or Python)
A programming language
Runs your code: data, models, figures


RStudio
An IDE
Where you write code and documents


Quarto
A publishing system
Turns your .qmd into a finished document






You use them together:

write a .qmd in RStudio,
render it from the terminal, and
Quarto has R run your code and builds the document around the results.
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.4 What happens when you render
quarto render report.qmd






flowchart LR
  Q[".qmd<br/>text + code"] --> E["engine<br/>runs the code"]
  E --> M[".md<br/>text + results"]
  M --> P["Pandoc<br/>converts"]
  P --> O["HTML, Word,<br/>PDF, slides"]










An engine runs your code chunks: knitr for R, Jupyter for Python
Your numbers, tables, and figures are woven into the text
Pandoc converts the result to the format you asked for




The engine runs your code in a fresh session,

not in your RStudio console.
Remember this; it matters in the next unit.
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.5 Why use Quarto?







The old way
With Quarto




Copy numbers from the console into Word, then they drift out of date when the data change
Text and code live together; numbers are computed every time you render


Rebuild the same figure for the report, the slides, and the paper
One source, many formats


Type citations by hand and renumber figures when you reorder them
Citations come from a .bib file; figure and table numbers update themselves


“How did I get this result?”
Rendering re-runs everything from scratch, so the document is the record


Binary files that Git can’t compare
Plain text that works with Git
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.6 A few quick notes
Quarto is its own program.

Like Git, you run it from the terminal, and every command starts with quarto.
It works the same whether you edit in RStudio, Positron, VS Code, or Jupyter.




It is not just for R.

If your project uses Python, you can use Quarto the same way.
Code chunks just say {python} instead of {r}.




Coming from R Markdown?

Quarto is its successor.
Most of what you know carries over, and your .Rmd files still work.
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.7 Source vs. output











File
What it is
What you do with it




report.qmd
The source
Write and edit it; commit it to Git


report.html
The output
Read and share it; never edit it by hand






Quarto rebuilds the output from scratch every time you render, so any edits you make to the HTML will be overwritten.



To change the output, change the source and render again.
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?
text:
1.8 Where we are
We have:

Defined Quarto as a publishing system, separate from R and RStudio
Seen what happens when you render
Seen why it beats copy and paste for reports, slides, and papers











ImportantNext up



Time to write one. Next we will build our first Quarto report about a Madison favorite: ice on Lake Mendota.
crumbs: 1  Quarto Workshop: What Is Quarto?

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.1 When is Lake Mendota frozen?
The Wisconsin State Climatology Office decides each winter.
For Mendota, one of their rules is a bit unusual:
The story, handed down by oral tradition:
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
Can you row a boat from Picnic Point to Maple Bluff?
If not, the lake is frozen.






UW limnologists E. A. Birge and Chancey Juday were often out on the lake in a rowboat
The ice along that line decided whether they could row a case of beer to their friends in Maple Bluff
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.2 Our data
Observers have recorded ice on Lake Mendota every winter since the 1850s.



You downloaded them to data/mendota_ice.csv, one row per winter:

winter: the winter, e.g., 1855-56
year: the year that winter ended
ice_days: days the lake was frozen




171 winters, from 1855-56 to 2025-26.

The question for our report: is ice cover declining?
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.3 What we will build
One file, report.qmd, with:

A YAML header: title, author, date, format
Text written in markdown: headings, paragraphs, lists
Code chunks that load the data and draw a figure
Inline R: numbers in sentences, computed from the data




We will render it after each step so you can see what changed.
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.4 Create the file
In the terminal, move into your repo and create an empty file:
cd ~/github/mendota_ice
touch report.qmd



Then open report.qmd in RStudio:

Use the Files pane, or File → Open File
It is a plain-text file, like an .R script
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
section: 2.5 The YAML (“Yet Another Markup Language”) header
text:
2.5 The YAML (“Yet Another Markup Language”) header
Type this at the very top of report.qmd:
---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: html
---



The header sits between two lines of ---

Each line is a key: value pair
format: html says what to build
date: today fills in the date each time you render
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.6 Render it
Back in the terminal:
quarto render report.qmd



Quarto writes report.html next to your .qmd.

Open it in your browser
In RStudio: click it in the Files pane → View in Web Browser




So far, just a title, author, and date.

Each time you change the .qmd, render again and reload the page
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.7 Markdown: headings, text, and lists
Below the YAML header, add:
## Background

Lake Mendota has been watched for ice since the **1850s**.

For each winter, the record notes:

- the date the lake froze
- the date it opened

## Ice cover over time




## is a section heading, ### a subsection
Put a space after the #
Start at ##; the YAML title is already the top level
**bold** makes text bold
A line starting with - is a list item
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.8 Blank lines matter
If you leave out the blank line before the list (Don’t do this step today)
For each winter, the record notes:
- the date the lake froze
- the date it opened



You get one run-on paragraph:

For each winter, the record notes: - the date the lake froze - the date it opened




Markdown needs a blank line:

before a list
before and after a heading
between paragraphs
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.9 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add the headings, text, and list from the last few slides
Render with quarto render report.qmd
Reload report.html and check that the list is a list
(Try later) Remove the blank line above the list items, render again, and see what breaks
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.10 Code chunks
R code goes in a code chunk:
```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
ice <- read_csv("data/mendota_ice.csv")
```




Starts with ```{r} and ends with ```
Lines starting with #| are chunk options
label names the chunk (use snake_case; not always required but helps when debugging)




Add this chunk just below the YAML header, then render.

A setup chunk at the top loads packages and data for the whole document
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.11 Hide the messages
Your readers do not need these in your report:

the tidyverse startup messages
the column messages from read_csv()




Add one option to the setup chunk:
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
ice <- read_csv("data/mendota_ice.csv")
```




message: false hides messages; the code still runs




Want to hide the chunk completely?

include: false runs the code but shows neither the code nor its output
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.12 Add a figure
Under ## Ice cover over time, add a chunk:
```{r}
#| label: ice_plot

ice |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = ice_days)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Winter (year it ended)", y = "Days of ice cover") +
  theme_minimal()
```



Render again.

Quarto runs the chunk and puts the figure right below the code
It also makes a report_files/ folder for the image; more on that in the next unit
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.13 The figure in your report













Lots of year-to-year variation
But the trend is down
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.14 Inline R
Do the work in a chunk:
```{r}
#| label: means

mean_1800s <- ice |> filter(year < 1900) |> pull(ice_days) |> mean() |> round()
mean_recent <- ice |> filter(year >= 2000) |> pull(ice_days) |> mean() |> round()
```



Then put the results in your sentences with inline R:
Before 1900, the lake averaged `r mean_1800s` days of ice.
Since 2000, it has averaged `r mean_recent`.

Backtick, the letter r, a space, then R code, then a closing backtick
Keep inline R short; do the work in a chunk


Before 1900, the lake averaged 114 days of ice. Since 2000, it has averaged 81.
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
section: 2.15 Render runs in a fresh session
text:
2.15 Render runs in a fresh session
In the RStudio console, run:
n_winters <- 171



Then add a sentence to report.qmd and render:
There are `r n_winters` winters in the record.



n_winters exists in your console.

So why will this fail?
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.16 The error
Error in eval(parse_only(code), envir = envir) :
  object 'n_winters' not found

Quitting from report.qmd:44-44
Execution halted



quarto render runs your code in a fresh R session.

It cannot see anything in your console
Not even chunks you ran in RStudio with the green ▶
Every object the report uses must be created in the report




This is a feature:

If it renders, anyone with your .qmd and data can rebuild it




To fix it:

Create it in the report: add n_winters <- nrow(ice) to a chunk above the sentence
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.17 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add the means chunk and the two sentences with inline R
Add one more sentence: how many days of ice in the shortest winter on record? (Hint: min(ice$ice_days))
Render, and check the numbers in report.html
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.18 Your turn: what to type
Below the means chunk, your text should look like this:
Before 1900, the lake averaged `r mean_1800s` days of ice.
Since 2000, it has averaged `r mean_recent`.

The shortest winter on record had `r min(ice$ice_days)` days of ice.




Before 1900, the lake averaged 114 days of ice. Since 2000, it has averaged 81.
The shortest winter on record had 21 days of ice.




Still getting an error?

The sentences must come after the means chunk; code runs top to bottom
Delete or fix the n_winters sentence from the last demo
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report
text:
2.19 Where we are
We have:

Written a YAML header that sets the title, author, date, and format
Used markdown for headings, text, bold, and lists
Run R code in chunks, and hidden messages with chunk options
Put computed numbers in sentences with inline R
Seen that quarto render runs in a fresh session











ImportantNext up



Our report works, but it is spread across an HTML file and a folder. Next we will render it to one self-contained file and publish it online.
crumbs: 2  Quarto Workshop: Your First Quarto Report

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.1 Two ways to share
Once your report renders, you can share it as:
We will do both in this unit.

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
a file: email it, post it on Canvas
a URL: publish it online

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.2 What render made
ls
data  report.html  report.qmd  report_files




report.html is the page
report_files/ holds the figure and the page’s styling




Email someone just report.html:

the figure and styling are missing

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.3 One self-contained file
Change format: in your YAML header:
---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---




html moves to its own line, indented under format:
YAML cares about indentation; use two spaces per level
embed-resources: true packs the figure and styling into the HTML file

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.4 Render again
quarto render report.qmd
ls
data  report.html  report.qmd




report_files/ is gone
report.html is now one file you can email or post
It is bigger (about 1.3 MB), because everything is inside it

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.5 Other formats, one flag
The same .qmd can become other formats:
quarto render report.qmd --to docx
quarto render report.qmd --to typst




docx: a Word document
typst: a PDF, with no LaTeX needed
More on Word output in the paper unit

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.6 Posit Connect Cloud
Posit Connect Cloud hosts documents online for free.

You made an account before the workshop




On the free plan, everything you publish is public:

Anyone with the link can see it
It is listed on your public profile page
This is true even if your GitHub repo is private
Never publish private or sensitive data

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.7 Publish
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud report.qmd



What happens:

Quarto renders the report on your computer
It uploads only the output
Connect Cloud never runs your code

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.8 First time only: authorize
Quarto first asks to Authorize:

Press Enter
Quarto prints an authorization code and opens your browser
Log in to Connect Cloud if asked, then approve the request




Quarto saves the authorization on your computer.

You will not need to do this again on this computer

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.9 Your report is live
When it finishes, Quarto prints the URL and opens it:
Published: https://connect.posit.cloud/your_name/content/...




Share this link with anyone
The title on Connect Cloud comes from title: in your YAML




The title is set only on the first publish.

To rename it later, use the Connect Cloud website

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.10 Update it
Change your report, then run the same command:
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud report.qmd



Quarto asks Publish update to:

The first choice is your report’s URL; press Enter
Don’t choose “Add a new destination”; that makes a second copy




How does Quarto remember the URL?

The first publish created _publish.yml next to your report
It records where report.qmd was published
Keep it, and don’t edit it

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.11 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add a sentence with the longest winter on record (Hint: max(ice$ice_days))
Publish the update with quarto publish posit-connect-cloud report.qmd
Reload your report’s URL and find your new sentence

title: 3  Render and Publish
text:
3.12 Where we are
We have:

Rendered the report to one self-contained HTML file
Seen that one flag switches the output to Word or PDF
Published the report to Posit Connect Cloud
Updated it at the same URL











ImportantNext up



Reports are one product. Next we will turn the same kind of document into a slide deck.

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.1 Your report is almost a deck
In the terminal, copy your report:
In slides.qmd, replace the format: lines with one line:
Render, then open slides.html in your browser:

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
cp report.qmd slides.qmd




---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: revealjs
---




revealjs is Quarto’s format for slides in a web browser
Yes, this copies your code; the paper unit comes back to that





quarto render slides.qmd

Use the arrow keys to move between slides

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.2 What you got
You changed one line, and:

The YAML header made a title slide
Each ## heading started a new slide
The code is gone: decks hide code by default




But one slide has a problem:

The figure shares its slide with your three sentences
Quarto shrinks the figure to make room for them

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.3 One idea per slide
Add a heading just above your sentences:
## The numbers

Before 1900, the lake averaged `r mean_1800s` days of ice.
Since 2000, it has averaged `r mean_recent`.




The sentences move to a new slide
The figure now has its slide to itself, and it grows to fill it




Want a new slide without a title?

Put --- on a line by itself, with blank lines around it

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.4 Bullets and pauses
Slides read better as short bullets than as sentences:
## The numbers

- Before 1900: `r mean_1800s` days of ice per winter
- Since 2000: `r mean_recent` days

. . .

- Shortest winter: `r min(ice$ice_days)` days
- Longest winter: `r max(ice$ice_days)` days



. . . on a line by itself is a pause.

The slide shows everything above it first
Press → to show the rest
Keep blank lines around it

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.5 Speaker notes
At the bottom of a slide, add:
::: {.notes}
About a month less ice than in the 1800s.
:::




Everything between ::: {.notes} and ::: is a note
Your audience doesn’t see notes




Press S for speaker view:

Your notes, a timer, and the next slide
If nothing opens, allow pop-ups for the page

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.6 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add the ## The numbers heading, render, and check that the figure has its own slide
Turn your sentences into bullets, with a . . . pause
Add a speaker note to one slide, render, and press S

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.7 Optional: publish your deck
First, give your deck its own title in the YAML header:
title: "Less Ice on Lake Mendota"

Connect Cloud takes the title from your YAML, but only on the first publish
Your report already uses “Ice Cover on Lake Mendota”




Then publish, just like the report:
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud slides.qmd

The deck gets its own URL
_publish.yml adds a second entry, for slides.qmd

title: 4  Slide Decks
text:
4.8 Where we are
We have:

Turned the report into a slide deck by changing format:
Split slides with ## headings, so each idea gets its own slide
Added bullets, pauses, and speaker notes











ImportantNext up



A project often goes from report, to slides for a conference talk, to a paper. Next we will write the paper.

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.1 What a paper needs
A paper needs things a report doesn’t:
And usually a Word file:

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
Citations and a reference list in a required style
Numbered figures and tables you can refer to in the text
An abstract
No visible code






Co-authors edit it with track changes
Many journals ask for .docx

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.2 Start from your report
In the terminal, in your mendota_ice folder:
cp report.qmd paper.qmd




cp copies a file: first the original, then the new name
paper.qmd starts with everything your report has




Copying is fine for today, but now the same code lives in three files: report, slides, and paper.

Change one, and you must remember to change the other
The DRY unit shows how to keep the code in one place

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.3 A paper’s YAML header
Replace the YAML header at the top of paper.qmd:
---
title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
abstract: |
  Lake Mendota freezes for fewer days each winter than it did in the 1800s.
  We summarize more than 170 years of ice records.
format: docx
execute:
  echo: false
---




abstract: | starts a block; the indented lines below it are the abstract
format: docx builds a Word document
execute: echo: false hides all code; readers see only the results
No embed-resources needed; a Word file always holds its own figures

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.4 Render to Word
quarto render paper.qmd



Quarto writes paper.docx next to your .qmd.

Open it in Word (or Google Docs, or LibreOffice)




You should see:

The abstract under the title
Your sections, sentences, and figure
No code




On Windows, close paper.docx in Word before you render again.

Word locks open files, so Quarto can’t replace it

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.5 Citations need a .bib file
You downloaded refs.bib during setup. It holds one entry (shortened here):
@dataset{magnuson2026,
  author    = {Magnuson, J. J. and Carpenter, S. R. and Stanley, E. H.},
  title     = {{North Temperate Lakes LTER}: Ice Duration - ...},
  year      = {2026},
  publisher = {Environmental Data Initiative},
  doi       = {10.6073/pasta/6a95bee73799927cbafbf87393be7038},
  ...
}




magnuson2026 is the citation key; you cite the source with it
Get entries from Google Scholar (Cite → BibTeX), a journal’s “Export citation” link, or Zotero




Point your paper to the file; add to the YAML header:
bibliography: refs.bib

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.6 Citation style
Quarto’s default style is Chicago author-date.

For APA, add one more line to the YAML header:

bibliography: refs.bib
csl: https://www.zotero.org/styles/apa



A CSL (Citation Style Language) file describes one style.

Thousands of styles, including many journals, are at https://www.zotero.org/styles
With a URL, Quarto downloads the style each time you render, so you need internet
Working offline? Download the file once and use csl: apa.csl

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.7 Cite a source
In your Background section, add a citation to the first sentence:
Lake Mendota has been watched for ice since the **1850s** [@magnuson2026].






You type
Quarto writes




[@magnuson2026]
(Magnuson et al., 2026)


@magnuson2026
Magnuson et al. (2026)






At the very end of paper.qmd, add a heading:
## References

Quarto puts the reference list there, formatted in APA

title: 5  Writing a Paper
text:
5.8 Number the figure
Change the figure chunk’s label and add a caption:
```{r}
#| label: fig-ice_days
#| fig-cap: "Days of ice cover on Lake Mendota, by winter."

ice |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = ice_days)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Winter (year it ended)", y = "Days of ice cover") +
  theme_minimal()
```



Then refer to it in a sentence:
Ice cover has declined since the 1850s (@fig-ice_days).

The label must start with fig-; Quarto requires that hyphen (the rest stays snake_case)
Quarto numbers the figure and writes “Figure 1” for you

5.11 Your turn: check your paper
In paper.docx, look for (Magnuson et al., 2026), Figure 1, Table 1, and the reference list.



A typo doesn’t stop the render.

Quarto prints a WARNING in the terminal and keeps going
Read the render output, not just the Word file











You see
Fix




(magnuson?)
The key doesn’t match refs.bib; check spelling and the bibliography: line


?@fig-ice_days
The label and the reference must match exactly, and start with fig-


Code in the Word file
Check the indentation of echo: false under execute:

title: 5  Writing a Paper
section: 5.12 Word and PDF from one render
text:
5.12 Word and PDF from one render

format:
  docx: default
  typst:
    citeproc: true



quarto render paper.qmd now makes both paper.docx and paper.pdf.

default means “no extra options for this format”
Typst makes the PDF, with no LaTeX needed




Why citeproc: true?

Typst formats citations itself, and it can’t read a style from a URL
This tells it to use the same citation engine as the Word file

5.13 Where we are
We have:

Turned the report into a paper with a few YAML changes
Cited a source, with a reference list in APA style
Numbered a figure and a table, and referred to them in the text
Rendered to Word (and PDF)
